nameStory: The 'bur-reed' name comes from the plant's spiky, round seed heads that look like tiny medieval maces or burrs that might stick to your socks. The 'unbranched' part refers to how this species keeps its flowering stem simple and straight, unlike some of its cousins that branch out in multiple directions.
description: Unbranched bur-reed is an aquatic perennial that lives in shallow ponds, streams, and wetlands throughout New England. This water-loving plant can grow up to 6 feet long, with long, flat, strap-like leaves that either float on the water surface or stand upright above it. Its most distinctive feature is the unique ball-shaped flower clusters - spiky green spheres arranged along a single stem like beads on a string.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive round, spiky balls arranged in a line along the stem - white male flower balls sit above the green female seed balls, looking like tiny green sea urchins when developing

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, flat, ribbon-like leaves up to an inch wide that feel smooth and somewhat rubbery, either floating limply on water or standing stiffly erect above the surface

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single unbranched flowering stem rising from the water, distinguishing it from branching relatives - the whole plant has a clean, organized appearance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Green spiky balls mature into brown, burr-like seed heads that feel rough and prickly to the touch, each containing multiple small seeds

idTips.label: Leaf Base
idTips.description: Look for a triangular, ridged (keeled) base where leaves meet the stem - this keel feels like a tiny raised ridge running along the leaf bottom

habitat: Look for unbranched bur-reed in shallow, quiet waters throughout New England - pond edges, slow-moving streams, marshes, and wetland margins. It thrives in water 1-3 feet deep with muddy or sandy bottoms, often growing alongside cattails, arrowheads, and other wetland plants. You'll find it from sea level up into mountain ponds and beaver wetlands.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from underwater roots and begin growing toward the surface as water warms. Early leaves are often completely submerged and limp.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the distinctive spiky flower balls appear and leaves reach full size, either floating or standing erect above water.
seasonality.fall: Seed balls turn brown and spiky, becoming very obvious. Leaves may yellow but often remain green well into autumn.
seasonality.winter: Most above-water parts die back, but sometimes dried seed heads persist through ice, and the plant survives underwater as roots and rhizomes.

funFact: This plant is essentially a living gender-segregated apartment building - all the 'male' flower balls live on the upper floors while all the 'female' seed balls occupy the lower levels, ensuring that gravity helps the pollen fall from the males down to the females below!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with narrow-leaved bur-reed, but unbranched bur-reed has wider leaves (up to an inch) and that distinctive triangular keel at the leaf base that you can feel with your fingers. Memory trick: 'Unbranched has unkeeled leaves' - wait, that's backwards! 'Unbranched has the keel you can feel.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'European bur-reed,' this species is actually native to both Europe and North America - it's what botanists call 'circumboreal,' meaning it naturally occurs all around the northern parts of the globe. The European name likely stuck because it was first scientifically described from European specimens.
compareHints: Among New England's bur-reeds, unbranched bur-reed is distinguished by its single, straight flowering stem and relatively wide leaves with keeled bases. American bur-reed has narrower leaves without the keel, while big bur-reed lives up to its name with much larger, more robust growth. Branching bur-reed has multiple flowering branches rather than the single clean stem.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American bur-reed can be distinguished from its bur-reed relatives primarily by size and habitat - it's mid-sized compared to the massive big bur-reed or the tiny small bur-reed.
Big bur-reed stands out from other bur-reeds by being the largest and having the biggest, most impressive spiky seed heads - it's truly the giant of the group.
Floating bur-reed differs from its relatives by truly living up to its name - it floats more readily than American or big bur-reed, which tend to grow in shallower water with more erect stems.
Among New England's bur-reeds, this species has the narrowest leaves and is the most aquatic, rarely growing in anything but deep water.
Small bur-reed is much more delicate and usually stays submerged compared to its relatives like American bur-reed or big bur-reed, which stand tall above water like cattails.
Branching bur-reed is distinguished from other bur-reeds primarily by its branching flower arrangement - most other species like unbranched bur-reed keep their spiky balls in a simple single row.
